payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
The request an independent publisher makes of AI companies is usually modest. Credit the source. Name where the sentence came from. Nearly all of the machinery built to express that request attaches it to training, and training is the one channel that cannot deliver it.

The finding sits in the machine learning literature and almost never in the licensing conversation. A model that learns something during pretraining is typically oblivious to which document it learned it from. The team behind the source-aware training work put it plainly in 2024: standard pretraining practice neglects attribution, which is why models fail to produce reliable citations for what they know. That paper also demonstrates a fix, a recipe that binds document identifiers to the knowledge inside each document and then teaches the model to name one when asked. It works on curated data. Nobody has shipped it at frontier scale, and no license clause causes it to exist. Looking inside the model does not recover the source either.

Goodfire's interpretability research finds model internals far more readable than assumed. Its memorization test worked because the researcher planted the label himself.

A training license cannot deliver attribution

An attribution-conditioned training license states a preference accurately and delivers nothing mechanically. Suppose a lab honored one in full, trained on the corpus, and paid. The resulting model would still answer questions without naming the site, and not out of bad faith. The pathway from a fact in the weights back to the document it came from was never built into the model, and a clause in a file at the edge of a website does not construct one.

That matters for how a rights posture gets designed. A reservation of training rights is a legal instrument and succeeds or fails on legal grounds. Whether anyone gets credited is settled somewhere else.

Music has started paying for that somewhere else. Warner Music Group agreed in June to acquire Sureel AI, which it describes as creating an "AI DNA" for each work and tracing how models use its component parts. In July, Canada's SOCAN named Musical AI an approved partner for attribution, with technology that analyzes generated outputs and assesses how much influence specific recordings and compositions had on them. That is attribution as an estimate made after generation, and one of the companies making the estimates now belongs to a record company that is also among the rightsholders those estimates would pay.

The vendors already split the channels

Citations come from retrieval. When an assistant fetches a page while composing an answer, the source sits in the context window with an address attached, and naming it is trivial. The vendors have already split their crawling along that line, which is the strongest available evidence that the channels are genuinely different. OpenAI documents separate agents for three separate jobs: one that crawls for model training, one that indexes for the citation surface inside its search product, and one that fetches a specific page because a person asked it to. Each is controlled independently in robots.txt, so refusing training while remaining quotable is a configuration that exists.

There is a catch worth naming. Late in 2025 OpenAI narrowed the wording of its crawler documentation, and observers reading the change concluded that the robots.txt commitment now covers the training and search agents while no longer clearly covering the user-triggered one. If that reading is right, the channel that actually produces citations is the channel carrying the thinnest stated obligation. Anyone treating robots.txt as a finished instrument should know which of its lines a given vendor has agreed to honor.

The block that costs both ways

Blocking indiscriminately has a measured cost. Hangcheng Zhao and Ron Berman, working from Comscore panel data and commercial traffic estimates across the largest news publishers, found that publishers who added disallow rules for AI crawlers lost around 7 percent of weekly traffic within six weeks of doing so. Their central claim is blunter than the number. The most widely adopted publisher response to generative AI does not stop the traffic decline and may accelerate it.

The 7 percent figure is from the authors' April 2026 revision. Their first draft had reported 23 percent.

Reading that as an argument against reserving anything would be the wrong lesson. Without a reservation, mining in the EU is permitted by default and any condition has nothing to attach to, so the reservation preserves the ability to impose terms at all, even where the machines it addresses never fetch it. The narrower lesson is about which lever does which job. Reserve training, because that is where the legal right lives, and leave retrieval open, where the credit lives.

Which leaves an awkward position for anyone building rights infrastructure. The channel that can actually deliver attribution is the one nobody has drafted a license for, because it looks like ordinary reading and behaves like it. The channel everyone is writing terms for is the one where attribution is not technically available. Whether that inverts as retrieval-heavy systems become the default interface is an open question, and the answer will not arrive from the license files.

References

Khalifa, M., Wadden, D., Strubell, E., Lee, H., Wang, L., Beltagy, I., & Peng, H. "Source-Aware Training Enables Knowledge Attribution in Language Models." First Conference on Language Modeling, 2024 (arXiv:2404.01019). arxiv.org/abs/2404.01019

Cammarata, N. "Neural Networks Are Already Clean." Goodfire. Accessed October 2026. already-clean.goodfire.com

OpenAI. "Overview of OpenAI Crawlers." developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots

Zhao, H., & Berman, R. "Strategic Response of News Publishers to Generative AI." Working paper, revised April 2026 (arXiv:2512.24968). arxiv.org/abs/2512.24968

Warner Music Group. "Warner Music Group Acquires Sureel AI." PR Newswire, June 10, 2026. prnewswire.com

SOCAN. "SOCAN Announces Collaboration with Musical AI to Advance Music Creator Attribution, Remuneration and Transparency in AI." July 20, 2026. socan.com
